column3: text (what is reasonably well established about a major clade; ages are estimates)
Every man alive today descends on his father's side from one man who lived in Africa roughly 200,000 to 250,000 years ago; the deepest branches of the tree are still found mainly in Africa.
All paternal lines outside the oldest African branches pass through BT, which arose in Africa well over 100,000 years ago.
Haplogroup C is spread across Central and East Asia, Siberia and Australia, and among some Native American peoples; it is one of the lineages carried out of Africa about 60,000 to 70,000 years ago.
Haplogroup D is found mainly in Tibet, in Japan and in the Andaman Islands, a scattered pattern left by very early movements across Asia.
Haplogroup E arose in Africa or western Asia more than 60,000 years ago and is today the commonest paternal lineage in Africa.
E-M2 dominates in West and Central Africa and spread south and east with the Bantu expansion over the last 3,000 to 4,000 years.
E-M215 is common in East and North Africa and the Near East, and reached Europe with Neolithic and later movements.
E-M81 is the typical paternal lineage of the Berber-speaking peoples of North Africa.
E-V13 is the main European branch of E-M78; it is most common today in the Balkans, where it reaches a quarter or more of men in places, and it spread widely in the Bronze and Iron Ages.
Haplogroup G was the commonest paternal lineage among the farmers who brought agriculture from Anatolia into Europe about 8,000 years ago; today it is most frequent in the Caucasus.
Haplogroup H is found mainly in South Asia.

Haplogroup I formed in Europe or nearby more than 40,000 years ago and is the one major paternal lineage that grew up mostly in Europe; the Mesolithic hunter-gatherers of western Europe mostly carried I2.

I1 split from I2 about 27,000 years ago, yet every man who carries it today descends from one man who lived about 4,600 years ago, most likely in southern Scandinavia. It is commonest in Sweden, Norway, Denmark and Finland, reaching around a third of men in places, and came to Britain largely with Anglo-Saxon and Norse settlers.
I-L22 is one of the large branches of I1, concentrated today in Sweden, Norway and Finland; in Britain it turns up most often where Norse settlement was heavy.
I2 was the main paternal lineage of Europe's hunter-gatherers before farming arrived; its surviving branches are commonest today in the Balkans and in Sardinia.
I-L621 is the branch of I2 behind its high frequency in the Balkans and eastern Europe, where it expanded rapidly in the last 2,000 years.
Haplogroup J arose in western Asia and spread with early farming and the first cities of the Near East.
J1 is commonest in the Arabian Peninsula, the Levant and the Caucasus; one branch spread widely with Arabic-speaking populations.
J2 is common around the eastern Mediterranean, Anatolia, the Caucasus and Iran, and in southern Europe, and is linked to the spread of farming and early civilisations there.
Haplogroup L is found mainly in South Asia and Pakistan.
Haplogroup N is the typical paternal lineage of northern Eurasia; its branch N-L1026 reaches more than half of men among Finns and is frequent in the Baltic and among many Uralic-speaking peoples.
Haplogroup O is the dominant paternal lineage of East and Southeast Asia.
Haplogroup Q is found across Siberia and Central Asia and is the main paternal lineage of Native Americans.

R1a is very common in eastern Europe, where it reaches around half of men in Poland, Ukraine and Russia, and in Central and South Asia; ancient DNA ties its spread to Bronze Age herders of the Eurasian steppe.
R-Z282 is the European branch of R1a, carried by the Corded Ware people of the early Bronze Age.
R-Z93 is the Asian branch of R1a, spread by Bronze Age steppe peoples into Central and South Asia.
R1b is the commonest paternal lineage in western Europe.

Ancient DNA links the spread of R-M269 to Bronze Age migrations from the Pontic-Caspian steppe about 4,500 to 5,000 years ago, after which it largely replaced earlier paternal lineages in western Europe, Britain and Ireland included.
R-U106 is commonest in the Netherlands, Germany, England and Scandinavia.
R-L21 dominates in Ireland, Scotland and Wales, where it reaches more than half of men in many places.
R-DF27 is commonest in Iberia and southern France.
Haplogroup T is rare but widespread, from East Africa through the Near East to Europe.
The L lineages are African and the oldest on the maternal tree; L0 is common among the Khoe-San and in southern and eastern Africa.
L3 arose in East Africa, and every maternal line outside Africa descends from it through M and N, carried out of Africa roughly 60,000 to 70,000 years ago.
M is one of the two roots of maternal lines outside Africa; its branches dominate in South and East Asia and include C and D, two founding lineages of Native Americans.
N is the other root of maternal lines outside Africa; almost all European maternal lines descend from it.
R descends from N and gave rise to most of the maternal lineages of Europe and many in Asia.
H is the commonest maternal lineage in Europe, carried by around 40 percent of Europeans; it expanded after the last Ice Age and again with later migrations.

V is carried by about 4 percent of Europeans. It probably spread from a refuge in south-western Europe (Iberia and southern France) as the ice retreated after the last Ice Age, and it reaches its highest frequency among the Saami of northern Scandinavia, where around 40 percent carry it.
U is one of the oldest maternal lineages in Europe, older than the last Ice Age.
U5 was the commonest maternal lineage among Europe's Mesolithic hunter-gatherers; today about 7 to 10 percent of Europeans carry it, most often in Finland and among the Saami.
U4 occurs among Mesolithic hunter-gatherers and today in eastern Europe and western Siberia.
K, a branch of U8, is carried by about 6 percent of Europeans and is notably common among Ashkenazi Jews; it came into Europe with Neolithic farmers.
J is carried by about 1 in 10 Europeans and came into Europe from the Near East with the first farmers.
T is carried by about 1 in 10 Europeans and, like J, arrived with Neolithic farmers from the Near East.
I is found at low frequency across Europe and the Near East.
W is found at low frequency in Europe, the Near East and South Asia.
X is rare but widely scattered; its branch X2 occurs in Europe and the Near East and among some Native American peoples.
A is common in East Asia and Siberia and is one of the founding maternal lineages of Native Americans.
F is common in East and Southeast Asia.
